{{About|the partial inverse of a matrix|the partial inverse of a function|Inverse function#Partial inverses}}

== Definition ==
In [[linear algebra]] and [[statistics]], the '''partial inverse''' of a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] is an operation related to [[Gaussian elimination]] which has applications in [[numerical analysis]], [[statistics]] and [[physics]]. It is also known by various authors as the '''principal pivot transform''', or as the '''sweep''', '''gyration''', or '''exchange''' operator, represented by <math>\mathrm{inv}_k</math> if restricted to blocks along the [[main diagonal]], or by <math>\hat{Y}_{k\ell}</math> if considering the general case of any arbitrary block from the matrix.<ref name="lima">{{Cite journal
 | last1 = Lima
 | first1 = Dennis
 | last2 = Al-Kuwari
 | first2 = Saif
 | title = Unitarization of pseudo-unitary quantum circuits in the S-matrix framework
 | journal = Physica Scripta
 | volume = 99
 | issue = 4
 | year = 2024
 | pages = 045202
 | doi = 10.1088/1402-4896/ad28f7
}}</ref>

Given an <math> n \times n </math> matrix <math> A</math> over a vector space <math>V</math> partitioned into blocks:

:<math> A = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix} </math>

If <math>A_{11}</math> is invertible, then the partial inverse of <math>A</math> around the '''pivot block''' <math>A_{11}</math> is created by inverting <math>A_{11}</math>, putting the [[Schur complement]] <math>A / A_{11}</math> in place of <math>A_{22}</math>, and adjusting the off-diagonal elements accordingly:<ref name="ppt"/>

:<math> \operatorname{inv}_1 A = \begin{pmatrix} (A_{11})^{-1} & - (A_{11})^{-1} A_{12} \\ A_{21}  (A_{11})^{-1} & A_{22} - A_{21}  (A_{11})^{-1}A_{12} \end{pmatrix} </math>

Conceptually, partial inversion corresponds to a rotation<ref name="TT">[https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2015/10/07/sweeping-a-matrix-rotates-its-graph/ Sweeping a matrix rotates its graph],</ref> of the [[Graph of a function|graph]] of the matrix <math> (X, AX) \in V \times V</math>, such that, for conformally-partitioned column matrices <math>(x_1, x_2)^T</math> and <math>(y_1, y_2)^T</math>:<ref name="ppt">Tsatsomeros, M. J. (2000). Principal pivot transforms: properties and applications. Linear Algebra and its Applications, 307 (1-3), 151–165.</ref>

:<math> A \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix} \Leftrightarrow 
\operatorname{inv}_1(A) \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix} </math>

As defined this way, this operator is its own inverse: <math> \operatorname{inv}_k(\operatorname{inv}_k(A)) = A </math>, and if the pivot block <math>A_{11}</math> is chosen to be the entire matrix, then the transform simply gives the matrix inverse <math>A^{-1}</math>. Note that some authors define a related operation (under one of the other names) which is not an inverse per se; particularly, one common definition instead has <math>(\operatorname{inv}_k)^2 (A) = -A</math>.

The transform is often presented as a pivot around a single non-zero element <math>a_{kk}</math>, in which case one has

:<math>
\left[ \operatorname{inv}_k (A) \right]_{ij} = \begin{cases} 
\frac{1}{a_{kk}} & i = j = k \\
-\frac{a_{kj}}{a_{kk}} & i = k, j \neq k \\
\frac{a_{ik}}{a_{kk}} & i \neq k, j = k \\
a_{ij} - \frac{a_{ik} a_{kj}}{a_{kk}} & i \neq k, j \neq k
\end{cases}
</math>

== Properties ==
=== Restricted Partial Inversion ===
Restricted partial inverses obey a number of nice properties:<ref name="Leeuw">[http://deleeuwpdx.net/pubfolders/pivot/pivot.pdf Exceedingly Simple Principal Pivot Transforms]</ref>
* inversions around different blocks commute, so larger pivots may be built up from sequences of smaller ones.
* partial inversion preserves the space of symmetric matrices.
* partial inversion over a block of size 1 along the main diagonal of a matrix can be expressed in terms of a composition of an identity operator, a [[commutator]] operator and a special commutator that resembles the [[Yang-Baxter equation]].<ref name="lima"/>

=== General Partial Inversion ===
The general partial inversion group <math>Z(n) </math> of generators <math>\hat{Y}_{k\ell}</math> that act on objects of size <math>n</math> is a [[non-Abelian group]], since it is a composition of the [[symmetric group]] <math>S(n)</math>, which is non-Abelian, with the restricted partial inversion group <math> V(n) </math> (which is Abelian)
.<ref name="lima"/> <math>Z(n)</math> admits representations of the [[dihedral group]] and the [[unitary group]].

<math>
Z(n) = V(n) \times S(n)
</math>

==== Commutators ====
It was suggested in <ref name="lima"/> that a composition <math>\hat{Y}_{ik}\hat{Y}_{j\ell} </math> only commutes if their row indices are different and their column indices are also different:

<math>
\text{[} \hat{Y}_{ik}, \hat{Y}_{j\ell} \text{]} =0 \quad \text{iff} \quad  i \neq j \quad  \mathrm{and}\quad k \neq \ell.
</math>

The [[Yang-Baxter equation]] <math>
ABA = BAB
</math> occurs as a constraint<ref name="lima"/> of generators of <math>Z(n) </math>, by introducing the substitutions

<math>\begin{align}
A =\hat{Y}_{i-1,i},
\\B= \hat{Y}_{i+1,i}.
\end{align}
</math>

==== Dihedral Group Representation ====

Compositions of matrix inverse along the main diagonal, <math>\hat{y}_1</math> and a generalized inverse along the secondary diagonal <math>\hat{y}_2</math> form a representation of the [[dihedral group]], <math> D(n)</math>:

<math>
\begin{align}
\hat{y}_1 &= \prod_{k=1}^{n} \mathrm{inv}_k,
\\ \hat{y}_2 &= \prod_{k=1}^{n}\hat{Y}_{k,n-k+1},
\\ \hat{y}_3  &:= \hat{y}_1\hat{y}_2 = \hat{J},
\\ \text{[}\hat{y}_k,\, \hat{y}_\ell\text{]} &= 0, \quad \mathrm{with} \quad  k,\ell \in \{1,2,3\},
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>\hat{J} </math> is a similarity transformation made of the reverse [[permutation matrix]].

In three dimensions, the [[dihedral group]] <math>D(3)</math> over a matrix <math>M</math> is represented in terms of the identity <math>\hat{I} </math> operator and the generators <math>\hat{y}_1,\hat{y}_2,\hat{y}_3 </math> as

<math>
\begin{align}
\hat{I}M &= M,
\\ \hat{y}_1 M &= \mathrm{inv}_3\,\mathrm{inv}_2\, \mathrm{inv}_1M = \hat{Y}_{33}\hat{Y}_{22}\hat{Y}_{11}M,
\\ \hat{y}_2 M &= \hat{Y}_{31}\hat{Y}_{22}\hat{Y}_{13}M,
\\ \hat{y}_3 M  &= 
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&1
\\0&1&0
\\1&0&0
\end{pmatrix}M
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&1
\\0&1&0
\\1&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}
</math>

==== Additional Properties ====
* A sequence of partial inversions and matrix powers defines the graph operation of Renormalized Growth,<ref name="lima"/> where the dimension of the matrix is kept constant, while the graph that represents it is interpreted to grow.

== Applications ==
=== Physics ===
In [[S-matrix theory]] and pseudo-unitary [[quantum mechanics]], partial inversion is used to map S-matrices to T-matrices, and, consequently, unitary matrices to Z-pseudo-unitary matrices.<ref name="lima"/>

=== Numerical Analysis ===
Use of the partial inverse in numerical analysis is due to the fact that there is some flexibility in the choices of pivots, allowing for non-invertible elements to be avoided, and because the operation of ''rotation'' (of the graph of the pivoted matrix) has better [[numerical stability]] than the ''shearing'' operation which is implicitly performed by Gaussian elimination.<ref name="TT" /> Use in statistics is due to the fact that the resulting matrix nicely decomposes into blocks which have useful meanings in the context of linear regression.<ref name="Leeuw"/>
